title: The night sky is dark because the universe had a beginning
body: If the universe were infinite, eternal and evenly filled with stars, every line of sight would eventually end on a star and the whole sky would blaze. That it doesn’t is Olbers’ paradox, posed by Kepler in 1610 and named after the German astronomer who described it in 1823. The resolution is that the universe is about **13.8 billion years old**, so we can only see stars whose light has had time to reach us, and the expansion of space stretches the light that does arrive, draining its energy. Edgar Allan Poe anticipated part of the answer in 1848.

slides.heading: The puzzle
slides.text: Imagine standing in an endless forest: wherever you look, your eye eventually meets a tree trunk. Stars in an infinite, ageless universe would do the same to the sky. Each shell of space farther out holds more stars, just enough to make up for their dimness.

events.text: Edmond Halley and Jean-Philippe de Chéseaux give it its mature form
Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers describes it, and it takes his name
Edgar Allan Poe’s Eureka anticipates part of the solution

slides.question: How old is the universe?
slides.explanation: About 13.8 billion years. The number of stars we can see is limited by that age, not by the size of the universe.

slides.label: years since the Big Bang, the limit on how far we can see
slides.text: The number of visible stars is limited by the age of the universe, not by its size.

slides.heading: Why the night sky is dark

steps.label: The universe began 13.8 billion years ago
Light from farther stars hasn’t arrived yet
The oldest glow is now invisible microwaves
To our eyes, the sky stays dark

slides.heading: The glow is still there
slides.text: Look far enough and every line of sight does end on something: the surface of last scattering, where the light of the Big Bang first escaped. Expansion has stretched that glow into microwaves, the cosmic microwave background, so to our eyes the sky stays dark.
